claims.claim: A checking account is a deposit account at a bank or credit union used for everyday money in and out: paychecks and transfers arrive, and bills, purchases, and withdrawals leave.
Money enters a checking account as deposits — cash, checks, or electronic payments such as direct-deposited paychecks — and the money is not always spendable immediately.

Cash deposited in person and checks for $225 or less deposited in person must generally be made available by the next business day; larger checks and deposits into very new accounts can be held longer.
A debit card spends money directly out of the linked checking account, so a purchase lowers the balance at the moment of the transaction.
Bills can be paid from a checking account by check, automatic (direct) debit, or online bill pay, and automatic payments can be stopped by contacting the merchant and the bank.

An overdraft occurs when a transaction goes through with more money than the account holds and the bank pays it anyway; the customer owes the shortfall plus overdraft fees, which many institutions charge at $30 or more per transaction.

Overdraft protection options include opting out of debit and ATM overdraft coverage (the card is declined and no fee applies) and linking the checking account to a savings account (the shortfall is covered by a transfer, usually for a fee smaller than an overdraft fee).

Practical ways to avoid overdrafts: track the balance carefully, sign up for low-balance alerts, know when scheduled payments such as rent and utility bills will be paid, and know when deposited money will be available.
FDIC deposit insurance protects money in checking and savings accounts at FDIC-insured banks automatically, up to at least $250,000 per depositor per bank, in the event the bank fails.

The FDIC is an independent agency created by Congress to maintain stability and public confidence in the nation's financial system, and its insurance covers checking accounts among other deposit accounts.

A checking account is a tool for moving everyday money in and out, not a place where money grows; the lesson frames this honestly and points money-set-aside topics to the savings-accounts sibling lesson.

conflictingEvidence: Fee amounts vary by institution: CFPB reports overdraft fees of $30 or more per transaction at many institutions, but does not state a universal figure; the lesson names fees generally and attributes the $30 figure to CFPB's 'many institutions' framing.

Deposit availability timing varies: CFPB gives next-business-day rules for cash and small checks with longer holds allowed for large checks and new accounts; the lesson states the general rule and avoids quoting exact hold schedules as universal.

Checking versus savings is a usage distinction, not a legal one: both are deposit accounts covered by the same deposit insurance; the lesson treats the difference as purpose (daily flow versus money set aside), which is consistent across sources, and leaves savings mechanics to the sibling topic.

The old CFPB ask-cfpb page 'What is a checking account?' is no longer served (404); the lesson's working definition is supported instead by the current CFPB bank-accounts hub, the CFPB bill-payment guide, and the FDIC deposit-insurance page.

sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. The hub frames checking accounts as everyday bank accounts and links how-to guides (online bill pay, stopping automatic payments, moving a checking account), overdraft-options guidance, and deposit-availability answers. Supports the working definition, the flow framing, and the named mechanics.

sourceRecords.title: Know your overdraft options
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Defines an overdraft (transaction paid with insufficient funds), states that many institutions charge $30 or more per overdraft transaction, describes opt-out and linked-savings-account options, and lists practical avoidance tips (track balance, low-balance alerts, know when scheduled payments and deposits land).

sourceRecords.title: How long can a bank or credit union hold funds I deposited?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Next-business-day availability for cash and in-person checks of $225 or less; longer holds permitted for larger checks, new accounts, and other conditions; mobile-check deposits may follow a different timetable. Supports the deposit-availability claim and the 'know when deposits clear' practice.

sourceRecords.title: A Newcomer's Guide to Managing Money: Ways to pay your bills
sourceRecords.notes: PDF downloaded via HTTP on 2026-08-21 and read with pdftotext. Describes paying bills from a checking account by check, automatic (direct) debit, and other methods, including how to stop automatic withdrawals (contact the merchant and the bank). Supports the bills-and-transfers mechanics.

sourceRecords.title: Deposit Insurance
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. States deposits are automatically insured to at least $250,000 at each FDIC-insured bank; insurance covers checking accounts, savings accounts, money market deposit accounts, and CDs; the FDIC is an independent agency created by Congress. Supports the insurance claims and the checking-as-deposit-account framing.
